summary: Describes a session authorization policy element, a piece of data carried in resource reservation signalling so network devices can check that a requested reservation was authorized for a particular session. It supports policy-based per-session authorization and admission control. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Before a theater lets you in, someone checks you have a ticket. This memo defines a kind of ticket stamp that travels with a network reservation, so routers can check it was approved before holding space.

questions: how to authorize a qos reservation per session
what is the session authorization policy element
how does rsvp session authorization work
how is the auth_session policy element authenticated
subtitle: A signed ticket that rides inside a network reservation request so routers can check the session was approved.

tldr.problem: A host can ask routers to reserve network resources, but the routers need a way to confirm that this particular session was actually authorized, otherwise service can be stolen.
tldr.mechanism: An authorizing entity gives the host an AUTH_SESSION policy element, a list of attributes (who authorized it, session ID, addresses, times, resources, authentication data), which the host copies into the Policy Data object of its reservation message for the router or policy server to verify.
tldr.outcome: Routers and policy servers can check integrity, replay protection and the authorized limits before admitting a reservation. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 3520 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2003. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Sessions Need Authorization
sections.content:
A host can use a resource reservation protocol such as RSVP to ask the network for specific service for a data flow. Requests generally result in resources being reserved in each router along the data path. Admission control is often based on user or application identity, but it is also valuable to control admission per session.

That requires information in the reservation message that can be used to verify the request. RFC 3520 defines the session authorization policy element (AUTH_SESSION) for this. The host obtains it from an authorizing entity through a session signaling protocol such as SIP, then inserts it into the reservation message. For RSVP it MUST be carried in the Policy Data object of a PATH message. Network elements verify it and then apply their admission policy.
sections.eli5: When you want a reserved seat, you first get a signed slip from the box office. You show the slip at the door, and the staff check it before letting you sit there.

sections.title: The AUTH_SESSION Policy Element and Its Attributes
sections.content:
The element follows the format of a POLICY_DATA object from RFC 2750 and has a 16-bit Length, a 16-bit P-Type (AUTH_SESSION = 0x04) and then a list of session authorization attributes. The length counts the whole element and MUST be a multiple of 4 octets.

Each attribute has a 16-bit length, an 8-bit X-Type, an 8-bit SubType and a value. Attributes are padded with zero bytes to a 4-octet boundary, and the length does not count the padding.

AUTH_ENT_ID
Identifies the entity that authorized the session. Sub-types include IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, FQDN, distinguished names, URI, Kerberos principal, X.509 v3 certificate and PGP certificate.
SESSION_ID
An identifier only the authorizing entity needs to interpret. It can be used for replay detection or to match the request to a policy decision.
SOURCE_ADDR and DEST_ADDR
The authorized addresses, and optionally one UDP port list and one TCP port list. If no port attribute is given, all ports are valid.
START_TIME and END_TIME
NTP timestamps for when the session starts and ends. A request that does not arrive within a few seconds of the start time SHOULD be rejected.
RESOURCES
What may be requested: a maximum bandwidth in kbps, an RSVP flow spec, an SDP media descriptor or a DSCP.
AUTHENTICATION_DATA
Signs everything before it. If present it MUST be the last attribute.
sections.eli5: The slip has labeled boxes: who signed it, a ticket number, where you are going, when it is good for, and how much you may use. A signature at the bottom proves nobody changed the boxes.

sections.title: Protecting the Element's Integrity
sections.content:
The algorithm used for AUTHENTICATION_DATA depends on the AUTH_ENT_ID sub-type. Three environments are described.

Shared symmetric keys. The identifier MUST be an address, FQDN, distinguished name or URI. The first 32 bits of the authentication data are a key ID, since several keys may be configured for one identifier. All implementations MUST support HMAC-MD5-128. Keys should be changed regularly, with overlapping lifetimes so that transitions are smooth. Key maintenance is otherwise out of scope, but implementations MUST at least allow manual key configuration.

Kerberos. The identifier MUST be a Kerberos principal. The router or policy server asks its local KDC for credentials for the authorizing entity, and the authorizing entity returns the authentication data (a 16 byte MD5 hash or 20 byte SHA-1 hash) in a KRB_SAFE message, so the element itself should not carry it. Implementations MUST support the des-cbc-md5 encryption type and the rsa-md5-des checksum type. Triple-DES SHOULD be used over single DES.

Public key. The identifier MUST be an X.509 v3 or PGP certificate. The authorizing entity signs with its private key and the verifier checks the certificate and signature. For X.509 the signature is carried in CMS signed-data, and for PGP in a Signature Packet. The RFC says this verification ensures integrity, non-repudiation and data origin.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to prove the slip is real. You can share a secret stamp, ask a trusted referee who vouches for the box office, or use a special signature only the box office can make.

sections.title: Which Fields Each Framework Model Needs
sections.content:
RFC 3521 describes a framework with four models for using the element, and the required fields differ for each.

  • Coupled model: only SESSION_ID MUST be present. The policy server SHOULD protect its integrity in transit.
  • Associated model, one policy server: SESSION_ID and AUTH_ENT_ID MUST be present, so the edge router knows which policy server to ask. If the router cannot tell whether the identity is a legitimate policy server in its domain, AUTHENTICATION_DATA MUST also be included to guard against redirection to a bogus authorizing entity.
  • Associated model, two policy servers: the contents are identical to the one-server case.
  • Non-associated model: the element must carry enough for the policy server to decide on its own: source and destination, the resources of each media stream, START_TIME, the authorizing entity and authentication data. END_TIME and port numbers MAY be added. All fields MUST match the resource request, and if one does not the request SHOULD be denied.
sections.eli5: Different theaters want different amounts of writing on the slip. Some only want the ticket number. Others want the whole story on it, because the door staff cannot call the box office.

sections.title: Processing Rules and Errors
sections.content:
The authorizing entity builds the element as required for the model in use. If authentication is needed it signs the element, and the message MUST include either a START_TIME or a SESSION_ID to prevent replay.

An RSVP host MUST include at most one AUTH_SESSION element in a message, and MUST copy the one it received into the POLICY_DATA object without modification. A policy-aware router SHOULD pass the message to the policy decision point (PDP) and wait; a policy-unaware router ignores policy data objects. The message is rejected if the PDP answers negatively.

The router or PDP checks that the element type is supported, verifies integrity using the method that matches the identity type, consults its local policy tables and verifies that the requested resources do not exceed the authorized QoS. Any supplementary information used for the decision MUST be obtained securely.

If verification fails, the PDP MUST return a policy control failure (Error Code = 02) and SHOULD include a policy data object with more detail. With RSVP, the enforcement point MUST put that object in the outgoing RSVP Error message.
sections.eli5: The guard checks the slip, then checks the rules. If something is wrong, the guard sends you back with a note saying what failed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The stated purpose is to prevent theft of service. Replay attacks MUST be prevented. In the non-associated model the element MUST include START_TIME and policy servers MUST support NTP so their clocks agree. In every other model the policy server uses SESSION_ID to correlate the request with a known authorized session, and a replayed element MUST be detected and rejected.

In untrusted environments AUTHENTICATION_DATA MUST be included. The RFC prefers shared symmetric keys where possible because they keep the element small, which matters especially over the air in wireless networks, and every implementation MUST support them. Kerberos is the next choice and needs only the principal and realm name. Public key authentication offers high security and good scalability, but the credentials in the element make it larger.
sections.eli5: A ticket must not work twice. So the slip carries a time or a number the box office can check, and a signature so nobody can forge it.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The AUTH_SESSION policy element type is assigned the value 0x04. The attribute types are numbered 1 to 8 in the order AUTH_ENT_ID, SESSION_ID, SOURCE_ADDR, DEST_ADDR, START_TIME, END_TIME, RESOURCES and AUTHENTICATION_DATA.

For the attribute types and for each attribute's sub-types, values 0 to 127 are allocated by IETF Consensus and values 128 to 255 are reserved for Private Use and not assigned by IANA.
sections.eli5: Each kind of box on the slip gets a number from an official list, and some numbers are kept free for private use.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Actual attribute length in octets, excluding padding.

fields.name: X-Type
fields.desc: Attribute type, such as AUTH_ENT_ID (1) or RESOURCES (7).

items.label: SOURCE_ADDR
items.desc: Address specification for the session originator.

items.label: DEST_ADDR
items.desc: Address specification for the session end-point.

items.label: RESOURCES
items.desc: Resources the user is authorized to request.

items.label: AUTHENTICATION_DATA
items.desc: Authentication data of the policy element.
